name: arss
desc: Analyze a sound file into a spectrogram
why: Turning a sound file into a spectrogram is a satisfying audio-to-image transform, if an old one.

brief.what_it_is: ARSS (Analysis & Resynthesis Sound Spectrograph) is a command-line program that analyses a sound file into a spectrogram image. It can also synthesise a spectrogram, or any other user-created image, back into a sound. Its spectrograph uses a base-2 logarithmic frequency scale and a filter bank rather than the usual short-time Fourier transform. The homepage describes uses such as time stretching, pitch shifting, filtering with an image editor, and drawing sounds by hand.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as a tool for treating sound as an image, so that sounds can be stored as pictures, edited in image-editing programs, and turned back into audio. The author's stated aim is to leave room for experimentation: "Who knows what else, there's a lot of room for experimentation".
brief.how_it_works: Analysis runs the signal through overlapping logarithmic-scale Hann-window filter bank bands, then takes the magnitude of the analytic signal in each band as an envelope; each envelope becomes a horizontal line in the image, with amplitude mapped linearly to intensity. Synthesis upsamples each image line to the output sample rate and modulates it with either sine waves at each band's centre frequency or noise passed through the filter bank.

commands_seen.context: Compile command given in a July 2008 news item for building ARSS from source on Mac OS X. Links the libm and FFTW3 libraries and produces the arss binary.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs a C compiler (gcc), the math library, and FFTW3 (the -lfftw3 flag). The homepage gives no other setup steps. A 2008 news item mentions a Mac OS X Universal Binary with a double-click installer from a third party, and an AppleScript front end, also third party. Those are old and I did not check whether they still exist. The brew formula supplies the arss executable.
brief.standout: Instead of the STFT that most spectrographs use, ARSS uses a filter bank with envelope detection, closer to how analogue spectrographs worked. Because the image is a plain editable array of envelopes, the same tool that analyses also resynthesises, so you can paint or edit a spectrogram and hear the result.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage says "This site is in hiatus. Last updated on February 23rd, 2009". The latest release mentioned is ARSS 0.2.3 from May 30, 2008. The homepage says ARSS is "now superseded by Photosounder", a GUI program released December 17, 2008. The brew formula was not checked for a version date.
brief.caveats: The homepage is an old, hiatus-era project page with news dated 2008 to 2009, and it has no docs or install guide beyond the single gcc line. Platform details are dated: the Mac notes refer to PowerPC and Universal Binary builds. The author states the noise-synthesis volume may be "way off" for logarithmic bases other than 2 with linear frequency scale. The homepage's licence was not stated in the text I read. The Documentation, Download and Code pages were not followed because the page text did not expose their URLs.
quotes: The Analysis & Resynthesis Sound Spectrograph (formerly known as the Analysis & Reconstruction Sound Engine), or ARSS, is a program that analyses a sound file into a spectrogram and is able to synthesise this spectrogram, or any other user-created image, back into a sound.
ARSS is now superseded by Photosounder, which makes use of most of the techniques offered by ARSS in a simple to use and powerful graphical user interface and built in editor.
This site is in hiatus. Last updated on February 23rd, 2009
